snapshot.title: UPSC History: Swarajists, Simon & Nehru Report
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: 1923: Swaraj Party. 1927: Simon Commission. 1928: Nehru Report. Motilal: Report head. Lalaji: Simon protest death.

quick_notes.title: Swarajists vs No-Changers
quick_notes.detail: Pro-Changers (Swaraj Party): C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru. Wanted to "wreck the councils from within". No-Changers: Rajendra Prasad, Vallabhbhai Patel. Wanted to continue constructive work.
quick_notes.explanation: After Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922, the Indian National Congress split into two groups. One group, called the Swarajists, or Pro-Changers, was led by Chittaranjan Das and Motilal Nehru; they wanted to enter the British-run legislative councils and "wreck them from within" by obstructing all government work as a way to continue the struggle for freedom. The other group, called the No-Changers, was led by Rajendra Prasad and Vallabhbhai Patel; they believed the Congress should focus on "constructive work," such as promoting khadi (hand-spun cloth) and village uplift, and stay out of the councils entirely.

quick_notes.title: Simon Commission (1927)
quick_notes.detail: "All-White" commission sent to review constitutional reforms. Protested with "Simon Go Back". Lala Lajpat Rai died due to lathi charge during protests in Lahore.
quick_notes.explanation: The Simon Commission was a group of seven British members of Parliament sent to India in 1927 to review the country's constitutional reforms, which are changes to how the government is structured and run. Because the commission was "All-White," meaning every member was British and no Indian was included, Indians saw it as unfair and launched protests with the slogan "Simon Go Back," demanding the commission leave India. quick_notes.title: Nehru Report (1928)
quick_notes.detail: First Indian attempt at a constitution. Drafted by Motilal Nehru. Demands : Dominion Status, Joint Electorates with reserved seats, Fundamental Rights. Rejected by Muslim League (Jinnah's 14 Points).
quick_notes.explanation: The Nehru Report of 1928 was the first time Indians themselves wrote a complete plan for their own future constitution. It was drafted by a committee led by Motilal Nehru, the father of Jawaharlal Nehru. The report demanded that India be given Dominion Status, which means self-governing control over internal affairs while still being part of the British Empire, rather than full independence. It also proposed Joint Electorates, where Hindus and Muslims vote together in the same election, with Reserved Seats meaning a fixed number of seats in legislatures were set aside for Muslims based on their population. Additionally, the report included a list of Fundamental Rights (FR), which are basic freedoms like speech and religion that the government cannot take away. The Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, rejected this report and instead issued Jinnah's Fourteen Points in 1929, which demanded separate electorates for Muslims and more political safeguards.

quick_notes.title: Jinnah's 14 Points
quick_notes.detail: Response to Nehru Report. Demanded 1/3rd representation in Center and Residual powers to provinces. Marked the widening gap between INC and League.
quick_notes.explanation: The Nehru Report was a document published in 1928 by the Indian National Congress (INC) that proposed a constitution for India. In response, Muhammad Ali Jinnah, a leader of the All India Muslim League, presented his own set of demands in 1929, known as Jinnah's 14 Points. One key demand was that Muslims should get one-third of the seats in the central legislature, meaning they wanted a guaranteed share of power at the national level. Another demand was that residual powers—meaning all government authority not specifically given to the central government—should belong to the provinces, not the center. These demands showed that the Muslim League wanted strong protections for Muslim interests, while the INC wanted a strong central government. The disagreement over these points made the gap between the INC and the Muslim League wider, pushing them further apart.

quick_notes.title: Independence for India League
quick_notes.detail: Founded by Jawaharlal Nehru and S.C. Bose to demand "Purna Swaraj" (Complete Independence) instead of "Dominion Status".
quick_notes.explanation: The Independence for India League was a political group founded in 1928 by Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose. Its main goal was to demand "Purna Swaraj," which means complete independence from British rule. This was different from the goal of "Dominion Status," which would have kept India as a self-governing part of the British Empire, like Canada or Australia. The League argued that only full independence, not Dominion Status, was acceptable for India. It helped build public support for the idea of complete freedom, which later became the official demand of the Indian National Congress in 1929.

topic_title: UPSC History: Swarajists, Simon & Nehru Report
lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Politics of the Lull'. After NCM, the INC split into 'Pro-changers' (who wanted to enter councils) and 'No-changers'. We look at the formation of the Swaraj Party, the arrival of the 'All-White' Simon Commission, and India's first attempt at drafting a constitution—the Nehru Report. For UPSC, focus on the 'Demands of the Nehru Report' and why the youth (Nehru and Bose) were dissatisfied with 'Dominion Status'.
